paragraphs: Friend, this one's heavy, so let's sit with it for a minute. Lamentations 1 shows us a city that lost nearly everything, and the writer doesn't dress it up. Again and again he says there is "no one to comfort her" (Lamentations 1:2, 1:9, 1:17, 1:21). The Bible lets hurting people say it plainly, and that tells me God is not scared of our honest tears.

Here's the part that matters most. The poem owns the sin. It says "The LORD is righteous, yet I rebelled against His command" (Lamentations 1:18). But look who the cries go to: "Look, O LORD, on my affliction" (Lamentations 1:9). Even in the worst of it, the speaker keeps turning toward God, and that's the habit I want you to bake into your days.

So when your own life goes quiet and dark, don't hide it. Tell the LORD the whole thing, even the part that's your fault. I spent years in a drawer with nothing but dust to talk to, and I wish I'd known I could pour it all out to Someone who was listening. The poem ends with a heart laid bare (Lamentations 1:22), and honest is a fine place to start.
